content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes new augmentation techniques to improve representation learning using contrastive learning and experience replay to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in the problem of online continual learning. The idea is to use augmentation to add diverse views of data during training procedures to improve model generalization and the ability to distinguish unseen classes using contrastive learning. The approach also helps to use stored samples for experience replay more effectively. Experiments on three common benchmarks are performed to demonstrate that the proposed method is effective and compares favorably against existing works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The proposed method is sound.

2. Experiments consider the three most common benchmarks.

3. The paper is well-written and easy to follow and understands.


Weaknesses:


1. The ideas of sample selection and augmentation for CL have been explored before. Although the specific idea of using augmentation is new but similar works exist in the literature. In this sense, the proposed method is not unprecedented. The results are also somewhat predictable.

2. The values of M in table 1 are too large compared to the dataset size. I would like to see how effective the proposed method is when M is smaller.

3. Other than EWC, comparisons in Table 1 are done against methods based on using a memory buffer. I think it is necessary to include representative methods from other CL approaches for the sake of complete comparison.

4. There are methods that outperform the proposed method but are not included in the comparison. Consider for example:

- Online Continual Learning Via Candidates Voting

- GCR: Gradient Coreset based Replay Buffer Selection for Continual Learning
This will raise the concern that the proposed method is not much better compared to the prior works.

5. In the CL literature it is common to use other splitting frameworks using CIFAR100 and Mini-ImageNet. I would like to see the method's performance when 20 five-class tasks and 2 fifty-class tasks are used to see whether the method is effective in these cases.

6. In addition to average performance through the tasks, having learning curves, i.e., performance versus the task number, is common in the literature and presents the dynamic of learning. In my opinion, it is more informative that the final average performance. I think including them at least in the Appendix is helpful.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and I could follow the presentation. However, CL is a super-crowded field with some existing works using similar ideas. In this sense, the paper is not significantly novel. There are concerns about the results and the competitiveness of the proposed approach as listed above.  Details about implementation are offered but I think it will be difficult to reproduce results using only what is mentioned in the paper. The averages and standard deviations are computed using only 3 runs which might not be sufficient.
content.summary_of_the_review: There are many papers in the area of CL. New works in this area either should offer a new theoretical understanding or offer considerable performance improvements compared to the existing works. The paper lacks both aspects and despite being a sound work, it may not be good enough for a venue similar to ICLR.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors try to eliminate catastrophic forgetting in online continual learning, when adding new classes in the present model.

The main idea of the paper is to try to learn more generalised features, such that it can be readily suitable for the oncoming tasks. To be more concrete,  the authors proposes to utilise a strong data augmentation to boost the feature generalisability learnt by the contrastive learning. The proposed method first augments an image into K instances in which each instance is treated as belonging to different classes, then every instance generates two views. 

The experiments are conducted on three popular benchmarks, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and mini-imagenet datasets to prove the effectiveness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength]

The motivation of the proposed method is clear, and the paper is easy to understand and follow.

[Weakness]

The paper here focuses on the online incremental learning, which has a fixed size memory M to store the exemplars of the old/learnt classes, which is said for the purpose of experience replay. However, in the field of continual learning, I don't think keep a fraction of old data is a new and valuable setting. The most related continual learning methods choose not to use the old data at all, which is more practical. So can the paper be transferred into that setting? Since the main idea of this paper is to extract generalised features. 

And then it reminds me that, if for the purpose of save memory for storing the old data, maybe using dataset condensation is better, since it could use only a few training samples for training the whole model.

And what's more, this paper tries to extract more common knowledge, which is more like a kind of representation learning, which, maybe in a way, like a kind of combination. I don't see much relationship between it and continual learning.

At last, I see the contribution of this paper is based on the finding that adding some particular transformations (e.g. rotation or blur) into the transformation module would instead hurt the quality of learnt representations as these transformations cause more significant distortion to the input image (thus having the semantic shift).  Is there any proof of it. If it is just based on the observation, it can't be proved to be effective in the other datasets. (for example, in MNIST, I think cropping may hurt the semantic larger)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The quality of the paper is fair

The clarity of the paper is good

 And originality of the work is fair.
content.summary_of_the_review:
As a whole, my main concerns are:

● Can the proposed method work on the cases without old data? For saving memory, can it be replaced with dataset condensation?

● What is the difference between representation learning? Can it be directly applied in representation learning?

● Is there any evidence for the observation that rotation or blur would hurt semantic representation larger?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method to use data augmentation and contrastive loss for online continual learning. It also deals with data imbalance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
The writing is mostly well written. 

Weaknesses
a. The novelty is limited as using data augmentation and contrastive learning have been used in online continual learning in several papers before. E.g.,  
    [1]. Online Continual Learning through Mutual Information Maximization, ICML-2022. 
    [2]. Rainbow memory: Continual learning with a memory of diverse samples. CVPR-2021.
Many offline continual learning methods have also used data augmentation and contrastive learning to improve continual learning. E.g., 
    [3]. Prototype Augmentation and Self-Supervision for Incremental Learning. CVPR-2021. 
The following paper has considered unseen classes. 
    [4]. Continual Learning Based on OOD Detection and Task Masking. CVPR-2022 workshop on continual learning.  
b. Many existing methods have already considered data imbalance. E.g., 
    [5]. SS-IL: Separated Softmax for Incremental Learning. CVPR-2021
    [6]. Large Scale Incremental Learning. CVPR-2019. 
c. [1] and [2] should have been compared experimentally.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is mostly easy to understand. 
The novelty is limited. See the weaknesses above. 
I don't see the code submission.
content.summary_of_the_review: The main issue of this paper is that the authors aren’t aware of many existing papers that have already used data augmentation and contrastive learning in online and offline class-incremental learning and have already dealt with imbalance of training data. So, the novelty of the paper is limited. Several latest online continual learning methods are not compared.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an online continual learning model that leverages the contrasting semantically distinct augmentation. The paper mostly focuses on the robust representation learning to overcome the catastrophic forgetting. Weight aware sample balancing also helps to mitigate the issue of imbalance samples since current task data are larger however, the replay samples are small. The model is evaluated over the popular datasets for the medium and small scale datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1: The online CL problem is interesting and has a wide application in the streaming scenario.

2: The paper is written well and easy to follow. 

3: Expanding each sample into K classes using the K data augmentation is interesting, but not sure about the impact. 

4: Weight aware balance sampling is important because of the nature of the problem. 

Weakness:

1: The augmentation and contrastive learning are the key contribution but the proper ablations are not shown in the paper. Here Eq:6 and Eq:8 are the contrastive and CE loss and the model is trained jointly. How much weight each loss has and what are impact of the Eq:6 alone and Eq:8 alone are not shown in the paper. Does the “identity” mean that only CE is applied?

2: The ablation shows the improvement using the K class expansion but the exact intuitions are not clear. Why is expanding the single class into K class not degrading the CE result?

3: In the baseline Table-1, how did the author made the baseline? How the hyperparameter search are applied to the baseline model? 

4: There are some recent paper on the Online CL but these are not included in the baseline, even some paper author discussed here like [a,b]. Also, recent work [c,d] focuses on the robust representation learning these work should be compared for the fair evaluation of the proposed model.

5: The ablations are provided on a relatively smaller dataset, i.e. CIFAR10, where it is easy to expand the classes into K augmented class. Could you please provide the ablation result for the CIFAR100 dataset? 

[a] Meta-Learning Representations for Continual Learning, NeurIPS-19

[b] Mitigating Forgetting in Online Continual Learning via Instance-Aware Parameterization, NeurIPS-20

[c] Meta-Consolidation for Continual Learning, NeurIPS-20

[d] Knowledge Consolidation based Class Incremental Online Learning with Limited Data, IJCAI-21
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clear writing, and easy to understand.

The proposed model is somewhat novel.

Reproducibility: The code is shared.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Please refer to the strength and weakness section. 

The baseline evaluation and ablation is primary concern. Also, there are many online-CL papers (some author discussed) but not included in the baseline. Why?

For the fair evaluation of the model, the suggested online-CL paper should me included in the baseline.
